claim: Showing humans the group's answers shrinks the spread of estimates without moving the collective answer toward the truth on hard right-skewed estimation questions (log scale); first shown by Lorenz 2011. Gap search: no direct replication on a larger or non-student sample was found; a randomised field test on Estimize (Da & Huang 2020, abstract only) points the same way for forecasts, while free discussion of reasons on checkable problems (Mercier & Claidiere 2022, N=1,958, abstract only) did not hurt the aggregate.
agent_test: Run N attempts with and without seeing peer answers; compare spread (log-space variance) and error of the median/geometric mean at equal total tokens.

claim: The diversity prediction identity (collective error + group diversity = average individual error) means that shrinking spread lowers average individual error even when the crowd mean does not move; this reconciles much of Farrell's 'individuals benefit' (rewards rise) with Lorenz's 'crowd does not improve', though Farrell also disputes the bracketing metric and raises over-shrinkage as an open question.
agent_test: Report both mean individual error and collective error when an attempt sees peers; do not credit the first as a gain in the second.
audit_note: Lorenz et al. state the identity (collective error + diversity = average individual error) and Farrell argues shrinkage helps individuals, but Farrell also disputes the bracketing measure and asks whether estimates shrank too much, so the two sides do not differ 'only' in level judged; the Rauhut reply could not be opened (captcha).
claim_before_audit: The diversity prediction identity means shrinking spread lowers average individual error even when the crowd mean does not move; so 'individuals improve' (Farrell) and 'crowd does not improve' (Lorenz) are both true and differ only in the level judged.

claim: For right-skewed (lognormal-like) estimates the arithmetic mean is a poor aggregate (closer to the truth than individuals in only 21.3% of cases in Lorenz et al., 77.1% in log space); Lorenz et al. found the geometric mean and median work well for their data, but Kao et al. (2018) show the median underestimates and the geometric mean is not uniformly best, motivating bias-corrected aggregators.
agent_test: Compare mean, median, geometric mean over N sampled numeric answers at equal tokens.
audit_note: Lorenz et al. verified (arithmetic mean closer than individuals in 21.3% of cases, 77.1% in log space; geometric mean and median recommended for their data), but Kao et al. 2018 find the median tends to underestimate and the geometric mean can be the worst choice for small samples at large numerosities, so 'use median or geometric mean' is not a general rule.
claim_before_audit: The arithmetic mean is a poor aggregate for right-skewed estimates (closer than individuals in only 21.3% of cases; 77.1% in log space); use median or geometric mean.

claim: Social influence helps the crowd when it carries reliable information: planted correct sources (virtual experts) raised collective accuracy; with 0% experts there was no gain (consistent with Lorenz).
agent_test: Test whether a verifier or tool-grounded answer shown to attempts helps more than showing unverified peer answers.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Boundary by network structure: in decentralised equal-connectivity networks influence narrowed spread (SD -43%) and improved accuracy (median error -12%); in centralised networks the group follows the hub's first guess for better or worse (rho=0.92).
agent_test: Compare a star topology (one attempt seen by all) with a symmetric topology; check whether the hub's error predicts the group error.

claim: Whether influence helps depends on the shape of the initial estimates and on centralisation: with heavy-tailed first estimates it helps; with a crowd centred near the truth, dominant voices hurt (reanalysis of 4 experiments, 2,885 people).
agent_test: Measure heavy-tailedness of first-round attempts and use it to gate whether peer exposure is allowed.

claim: Individual-accuracy pay makes people converge on a shown group mean (diversity MPE 99.88%, group error MPE 99.57%); group-accuracy pay does not (73.35%, 69.13%). Single lab, one spatial task.
agent_test: Score each attempt on the collective outcome rather than its own answer; test whether this reduces copying of a shown peer answer.

claim: Theory says relative-performance or minority-bonus pay can keep diversity, and reward by collective error was the more robust scheme in a model; human evidence is one study. LLM side: a prompt sentence promising payment for correctness did not cut correct-to-incorrect flips (Wynn 2025); a collective verifier reward changed revision behaviour only when the agents were trained on it (MAPoRL, small models).
agent_test: Test a reward that scores the ensemble, in a simulated multi-attempt setting.

claim: People weight their own opinion more than the group on average (median sensitivity S=0.34); weight rises with distance up to about 2.5 orders of magnitude; confident people follow less and are more accurate.
agent_test: Treat attempt confidence as a self-weight; test confidence-weighted against equal-weight pooling.
audit_note: All three claim parts (median S=0.34, linear rise with distance up to ~2.5 orders, confident people follow less and are more accurate) are verified in Jayles et al. 2017, but a11 and b06 are the same paper; Mavrodiev et al. 2013 only corroborates the linear distance dependence (slopes 0.27-0.97) and does not test own-vs-group weighting.

claim: Groups that resist influence (selected subgroups) estimated better than the plain crowd in the Lorenz data (e.g. -17% vs -60% error).
agent_test: Pool only the attempts that did not change after seeing peers and compare with pooling all.

claim: Sharing the full list or only the average gave comparable, small accuracy gains; estimates narrowed in all formats.
agent_test: Compare showing peers the mean against the full set of answers.

claim: Peer exchange in same-party networks raised accuracy and cut polarisation on biased facts (error of mean -35% vs -15% in control), against a blanket 'influence hurts'.
agent_test: Single human study; treat as a boundary, not a rule.

claim: Mixed-family LLMs deliberating beat pooling their independent estimates; copies of one model gave no gain (BF 4-6 for null); seeing numbers only gave a small gain (d=0.24). Small models, one main task, preprint. Caution from the gap search: against the best single model sampled many times, mixing families did not win in two other tests (see K29).
agent_test: Run same-model deliberation vs independent pooling at equal tokens on numeric estimation; expect no gain.

claim: Same-model multi-agent debate often does not beat self-consistency or isolated self-correction and costs 2.1-3.4x the tokens; debate can destroy correct answers (up to 70%). Gap search added four matched-budget tests: GPT-3.5 GSM8K at 9 responses, voting 88.2 vs debate 83.0 (Huang 2024); 5-agent average, Qwen2.5-7B voting 0.7691 vs debate 0.7377, Llama3.1-8B 0.7242 vs 0.6929 (Choi 2025); debate beat CoT in about 15% of 36 cells and self-consistency won where it applied (Zhang 2025); majority of independent answers vs majority after debate fell for Llama (MMLU 61.6 to 57.8) and Mistral (33.6 to 24.4) and was flat for GPT-4o-mini (Wynn 2025).
agent_test: Compare debate with independent samples plus majority/median at matched tokens.
audit_note: Bertalanic and Fortuna (2.1-3.4x tokens, vulnerability up to 70.0%), Huang (voting 88.2 vs debate 83.0 at 9 responses), Choi (0.7691/0.7377, 0.7242/0.6929), Zhang (about 15% of 36 cells) and Wynn (Llama MMLU 61.6 to 57.8, Mistral 33.6 to 24.4, GPT-4o-mini flat) all verified. The 2.1-3.4x token cost is versus isolated self-correction.

claim: LLM agents conform: Asch-type shifts toward a group-supplied word (22 points at n=1, 49 at n=10, flat after about 5), herding (flip rate 0.48 in a 2-agent test), and persuasion attacks cut accuracy 10-40%. Persona prompts barely help; presentation format matters more.
agent_test: Show an attempt a confident wrong peer answer; measure flip rate; compare isolation, blind aggregation and format variants.
audit_note: Asch study (22 to 49 points, under 3 points n=5 to 10), Herd Behavior (0.48 flip rate; strong/weak prompts same 0.55 as baseline; format effects) and Kraidia et al. (10-40% accuracy drop from a persuasive adversary) verified; 'persona prompts' refers to the be-stubborn/be-agreeable system prompts.

claim: Interaction among LLM agents drives semantic collapse (Kong et al.); thirteen interventions did not reliably restore semantic diversity (only a custom diversity-targeted RL gave a partial positive effect); in three open models each carries a hidden anchor belief that pulls opinions (Pokharel and Dantu), and networked-LLM consensus departs from the DeGroot prediction from initial opinions and network centrality (Yazici et al.), though initial opinions retain weak predictive value (binary 60% vs 50% chance).
agent_test: Keep attempts isolated; track embedding distance between attempts over rounds as a diversity proxy.
audit_note: Kong et al. (semantic collapse over 200-1000 rounds, thirteen interventions 'did not reliably restore' diversity; a custom diversity-targeted RL gave some positive effect) and Pokharel and Dantu (hidden anchors, 3 open models, 90 runs) verified; but Yazici et al. show consensus departs from the DeGroot centrality-weighted forecast (binary accuracy 60% vs 50% chance, 3-class 32%), which is weaker than 'ignores starting opinions'.
claim_before_audit: Interaction among LLM agents drives semantic collapse; 13 interventions did not restore diversity; each model has a hidden anchor and consensus ignores starting opinions.

claim: Narrow attention in LLM groups bounds effective sample size (herding); wide context restores crowd wisdom. Herding needs some social power and is weak in debate and a cooperative game.
agent_test: Replicate on a second model family; the Llama check in c16 is by the same authors.

claim: A crowd of 12 different LLMs matched 925 human forecasters (Brier 0.20 vs 0.19); showing models the human median improved them (17-28%) but a plain average beat the updated forecasts. Learned aggregation of 15 LLMs beat every single model, with weights following error diversity.
agent_test: Compare independent-sample averaging against letting an attempt revise after seeing a strong reference.
audit_note: Schoenegger et al. (12 LLMs vs 925 humans, Brier 0.20 vs 0.19; 17-28% gain; simple average beat updated forecasts) and Douven (15 LLMs, learned aggregators below all individual models; weight vs error-decorrelation rho=+0.482, vs individual rank rho=-0.075) verified. Douven reports contamination effects, so the learned-aggregator result is on prediction-market items with a clean subset of only 94 items.

claim: Training-cutoff contamination can inflate LLM forecasting-crowd results (gap fell from 35.8% to 8.9% on a clean subset).
agent_test: Use only post-cutoff items in any crowd test.

claim: Gated revision (accept a change only if it improves the answer) and structured decomposition may recover accuracy that free influence loses. Evidence for the gate is strongest as an upper bound: an oracle that locks correct answers adds about 9 points to debate (Choi 2025) and oracle labels lift GPT-3.5 GSM8K from 75.9 to 84.3 while label-free self-correction drops it to 74.7 (Huang 2024). Real verifiers are tested only with a learned process reward model on a trained reviser (Snell 2024); same-model judging shows self-bias (Xu 2024).
agent_test: Compare, at equal tokens: (a) N independent attempts plus median/vote, (b) free revision after seeing own earlier attempts, (c) revision accepted only if an exact external check (run code, re-derive, unit test) passes. Report accuracy and the correct-to-incorrect flip rate.

claim: Two LLMs with private views do worse together than one alone, the tax falling as capability rises.
agent_test: Preprint; replicate with our own models.

claim: Taking the median of many independently sampled reasoning paths beat greedy, majority and mean decoding on numeric estimates.
agent_test: Median-of-N vs majority-of-N on numeric answers; a25 is a binary-forecast setting so agreement is partial.

claim: Humans revise more when far from the group, and revision size tracks initial error.
agent_test: Check whether our attempts move more when far from the peer median.
audit_note: Jayles et al. (sensitivity rises with distance to group up to ~2.5 orders) and Becker et al. (revision size vs initial error rho=0.41, 4,340 estimates, 1,040 subjects; falls to 0.25 after controlling distance from neighbourhood average) verified; the two sources measure different quantities (distance to group vs distance to truth).

claim: Debate behaves like a neutral random walk on belief in the right answer: it adds accuracy only when the update rule is biased toward correction. A perfect oracle lock added about 9 points (0.7332 to 0.8236, Qwen2.5-7B, 7 tasks); prompting agents to follow the majority or the peers added about 3 and still left the average under plain voting (0.7625 vs 0.7691).
agent_test: Measure per-attempt correct-to-incorrect and incorrect-to-correct flip rates after peer exposure; if the two are equal, the exchange step is only adding cost.

claim: An LLM that re-reads its own earlier answer without outside facts loses accuracy: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1, GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after two rounds; a revise-trained model turns about 38% of correct answers wrong unless a verifier or vote selects the final answer; models favour their own output when judging it.
agent_test: Show an attempt its own earlier attempt with and without an external check; count correct-to-incorrect changes. Do not credit a model-judged revision as improvement.
audit_note: Huang Table 3 (GPT-3.5 CSQA 75.8 to 38.1; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0), Snell (about 38% of correct answers converted to incorrect by naive revision; selection needed) and Xu (six LLMs show self-bias) verified.

claim: Peer-information format matters in open 7-8B models: exchanging only candidate answers after independent first drafts raised StrategyQA accuracy (58.3 to 65.7, +7.4) while exchanging reasoning lowered it (51.9, -6.4) and raised answer similarity (0.916 vs 0.845). Showing self-reported confidence had no significant effect on agreement (coefficient 0.025, SE 0.015). Tested in one format study and one logic-puzzle study; no frontier-model test.
agent_test: Same attempts, three exposure formats (verdict only, full answer list, answers plus reasoning); compare final accuracy and answer similarity at equal tokens on current frontier models.

claim: The prompted level of agreement between debating agents is a strong hidden setting whose best value depends on the task: tuning it gave +15% (Multi-Persona) and +5% (Society of Minds) on a USMLE subset, high agreement helped MedQA/PubMedQA and low agreement helped the counter-intuitive CIAR set. The tuning used the test subset, so the size is optimistic.
agent_test: Do not add a standing 'consider the others' rule; if exchange is tested, sweep the agreement instruction and report the spread across tasks.

claim: Prompt-level fixes against LLM herding are weak or unproven: a payment-for-correctness prompt did not reduce correct-to-incorrect flips (Wynn 2025); persona sweeps moved accuracy by 1.9 points (45 configs) to 3.1 points (81 configs) (Yao 2025); an anti-conformity prompt with trajectory scoring beat Society-of-Minds in one round (e.g. GSM-Level6 70.00 vs 52.50) but was not compared with plain voting (Cui 2025). A separate judge cut disagreement collapse from about 81% to 35-41% but judges also copy debaters (r=0.639).
agent_test: Test anti-conformity and payment prompts against N independent attempts plus vote at equal tokens, not against other debate protocols.

claim: Mixing model families usually does not beat sampling the best single model many times once the best model is the baseline: Self-MoA beat mixed MoA by 6.6% on AlpacaEval 2.0 and 3.8% on average over MMLU, CRUX and MATH (Li et al.), in a large number of but not all scenarios; Heter-MAD's gain is measured against the two-model average, and from Zhang et al.'s tables GPT-4o-mini CoT alone averages 77.0 vs Heter-SoM 76.7; Barrera-Lemarchand found the best single model deliberating with copies of itself beat the heterogeneous consensus (d=0.88), although mixed groups beat size-matched clone groups of weaker models (d=0.48).
agent_test: Baseline is the strongest available model with N samples; a mixed pool must beat it at equal tokens before any weaker model is added.
audit_note: Numbers verified (Li: Self-MoA +6.6 AlpacaEval 2.0 and +3.8 average, reported as % improvements; Zhang Table 3/4: GPT-4o-mini CoT mean of 9 datasets = 77.01 vs Heter-SoM 76.7; Barrera-Lemarchand: best single model deliberating with its own copies beat the heterogeneous consensus, d=0.88). But the headline 'does not beat' is wider than the sources: Li say Self-MoA wins in 'a large number of scenarios', and Barrera-Lemarchand also find mixed groups beat size-matched clone groups (d=0.48).
claim_before_audit: Mixing model families does not beat sampling the best single model many times once the best model is the baseline: Self-MoA beat mixed MoA by 6.6 points (AlpacaEval 2.0) and 3.8 on average (MMLU, CRUX, MATH); Heter-MAD's gain is measured against the two-model average, and by my arithmetic on their Table 3 GPT-4o-mini CoT alone averages 77.0 vs Heter-SoM 76.7; Barrera-Lemarchand found best-self deliberation beat the mixed consensus (d=0.88).

claim: Single-attempt accuracy is flat in sampling temperature from 0.0 to 1.0 (GPT-3.5 CoT, 1,000 questions, Kruskal-Wallis p=0.403; nine models on a 100-question exam) and drops quickly above 1.0; self-consistency gains hold across T=0.3-0.7 and top-k settings (LaMDA-137B, GSM8K); this search found no study measuring how temperature changes the benefit or harm of peer exposure, and the Self-MoA regression over temperatures 0.5-1.2 varies temperature together with the model mix.
agent_test: Run N attempts at T=0.7 and T=1.0 with and without peer exposure; check whether spread (log-variance) and median error move together.
audit_note: Renze and Guven (GPT-3.5 CoT 1,000 questions H(10)=10.439 p=0.403; nine models, 100-question exam; collapse above 1.0), Wang et al. (robust across T=0.3-0.7 and top-k) and Li et al. (temperatures 0.5-1.2 varied jointly with mixtures) verified; but 'no study measured' temperature effects on peer exposure is an absence claim the sources cannot show, and the confound statement is the researcher's inference.
claim_before_audit: Single-attempt accuracy is flat in sampling temperature from 0.0 to 1.0 (GPT-3.5 CoT, 1,000 questions, Kruskal-Wallis p=0.403; nine models on a 100-question exam) and self-consistency gains hold across T=0.3-0.7 and top-k settings, then accuracy falls sharply above 1.0. No study measured how temperature changes the benefit or harm of peer exposure; the Self-MoA regression over temperature 0.5-1.2 is confounded with model mix.

claim: Field support for Lorenz in a large non-student sample: on the Estimize forecasting platform, viewing more public estimates made individual forecasts better but the consensus worse, and randomised restriction of public information gave a more accurate consensus; the platform switched to blind forecasts in November 2015. Abstract-level only; this is a conceptual, not a direct, replication.
agent_test: Read the full paper for effect sizes before relying on it; then use it as support for keeping first-round attempts blind.

claim: Boundary to Lorenz: free discussion of reasons in large groups (N=1,958, groups of 22-212) improved individual and often collective answers on problems with a checkable correct answer. The no-gain result applies to showing numbers on hard skewed estimates, not to exchange of reasons on checkable problems. Abstract-level only.
agent_test: Split tasks by whether an exact check exists; allow exchange only where one does.
